statement: In 2026, geopolitical tensions and private credit stress are creating amplified volatility in global markets.
verification_notes: Core claim lacks two independent tier 1-3 sources.

statement: China's economic challenges, including a property downturn, pose significant credit risks in 2026.
verification_notes: Core claim lacks two independent tier 1-3 sources.

statement: Europe's fiscal policies in 2026 focus on growth through strategic investments in infrastructure and defense.
Regulatory shifts encourage a move from traditional bank loans to private credit solutions across Europe in 2026.
Margin compression in private credit is exacerbated by restrictive global trade policy changes.
verification_notes: Core claim lacks two independent tier 1-3 sources.

statement: The elimination of IEEPA tariffs has lowered the average effective tariff rate, impacting private credit risk assessments.
Increased tariffs are likely to affect manufacturing sectors more severely, which impacts associated private credit structures.
Global private credit AUM reached approximately $2.1 trillion by end-2025 (ACC survey of 49 managers); US market alone grew from $500B (2020) to $1.3T (2025), a +160% increase.
Preqin projects global private credit AUM to reach $4.5 trillion by 2030, requiring ~16% CAGR from 2025 levels.
European private credit market at ~$530B (2025) projected to reach $940B by 2030; corporate lending in Europe still ~70% bank-reliant vs ~20% in the US.

Fed Funds rate rose 542bps (0.08% to 5.50%) over 17 months (Mar 2022 - Jul 2023), then fell 125bps to 4.25% by Jan 2025; private credit mid-market all-in yield peaked at ~11.5% (Nov 2023) and compressed to ~9.75% (Dec 2025).
BDC total returns Jan 2023 to Dec 2025: ARCC +45.0%, OBDC +47.2%, GBDC +44.0%, FSK +31.6%, PFLT +17.2%; FSK max drawdown from ATH is -34.3% vs -8.7% for ARCC.
US private credit default rate (Fitch) rose from 0.8% (Q1 2022) to 5.7% peak (Q2 2025), settling to ~5.1% by Q4 2025.
Healthcare roll-up default rate reached 7.0% in 2024 (KBRA), the highest subsector; interest coverage 1.1x; $45B debt outstanding, $18-27B in BDC portfolios (4-6% of BDC assets).

Covenant-lite prevalence in private credit (2025): 50-55% of mega-deals (>$500M debt) entirely lack financial maintenance covenants; 30% of upper mid-market deals are cov-lite; only 8% in lower mid-market.
PIK loans peaked at approximately 10% of BDC interest income and 11-12% of BDC loan holdings by value in mid-2024, before declining as rate cuts eased distress.
EBITDA covenant cushions in private credit typically allow 30-40% EBITDA decline before triggering breach; lender conservative leverage view is 30-40% above sponsor-reported adjusted EBITDA.
IEEPA Liberation Day (April 2, 2025) triggered VIX spike from 20.9 (30-day avg) to 52.3 on April 8 (+150%), the largest volatility spike since COVID-19; HYG drew down -3.7% in the window.
Supreme Court ruled February 20, 2026 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs; Section 122 replacement tariff of 15% on all imports effective February 24, 2026 for 150 days (expires July 24, 2026).
Over 90% of tariff costs borne by US businesses and consumers per NY Fed research (2025); fabricated metals face 12% added cost under Section 122; auto tariffs remain at 5.6%.
China large-cap equity (FXI) fell -42.4% from January 2022 to October 2022 trough; recovered +16.8% vs January 2022 base by December 2025 following PBOC stimulus package (September 24, 2024).

Private credit illiquidity premium over public HY compressed from ~330bps (July 2023) to ~265bps (December 2025) as BSL markets tightened; LMM direct lending retains 100-150bps premium vs syndicated loans.
Fee drag at 12% gross IRR: closed-end fund (1.5% committed + 20% carry above 7% hurdle) returns ~9.0% net to LP; BDC/perpetual (1.0% + 20% carry) returns ~9.7% net.
Vintage 2022 private credit funds experienced approximately 2 additional quarters of J-curve extension compared to 2019/2021 vintages due to deployment during peak rate uncertainty.

NAV facility market grew from ~$50B (2019) to ~$400B (2025), +700% in 6 years; LTV typically 15-25% of portfolio NAV; cross-collateralization risk creates contagion across performing assets when one portfolio company defaults.
LMM direct lending spreads command SOFR+450 to SOFR+475bps, a 100-150bp premium over syndicated markets, with maintenance covenants and restrictions on additional debt.
Global private capital deal value reached $2.3 trillion as of November 30, 2025, the best year since 2021; transactions of $10B+ in a calendar year hit a record high (Preqin).
Private credit secondaries averaged 92% of NAV in H1 2025, up from 91% at end-2024
Senior direct lending secondary transactions cleared at 97–98% NAV (2–3% discount) in H1 2025
GP-led credit continuation vehicle transactions averaged ~98% of gross NAV in 2025
Asia fund credit secondaries trade at 30%+ discounts to NAV on average
2025 estimated total private credit secondary transaction volume is ~$20 billion, roughly doubling from 2024
GP-led credit secondaries grew 202% YoY in 2025 to $12 billion, surpassing LP-led volume for the first time
Credit secondaries as % of total AUM is ~1%, vs. PE market's 2–3% — indicating early market immaturity
Average private credit loan duration has extended from 2–3 years to 4–5 years, increasing LP demand for secondary exits
FXI is +11.4% vs. January 2022 levels and +93.6% from its October 2022 trough of $19.06
China HY property OAS remains at approximately 780bps (early 2026), vs. ~350bps pre-crisis — a 2.2× residual risk premium
FXI recovery (+11.4%) is decoupled from Chinese developer credit quality: equity driven by state banks, tech; not property sector
China Vanke entered restricted default in January 2026 when seeking to extend onshore bond payment deadline
China nationwide residential sales fell to 7.3 trillion yuan in 2025, lowest since 2015; property investment fell 17.2% YoY
Country Garden seeks Hong Kong court-backed restructuring targeting $12.7 billion debt reduction over 5 years
China property sector represents only 4% of Asian HY index after mass-index cleanup from ~35% at peak
CRE HY yield at 9.19% (B+ rated) vs EM HY benchmark 8.04% (BB- rated); H1 2025 return of +7.33% outperformed CEMBI Broad HY at +3.91%
FXI rolling correlation with HYG (US high yield) is stable at ~0.33 throughout 2021–2026, confirming persistent equity-credit decoupling
A&O Shearman warns of second-time defaults on restructured Chinese developer debt in 2026, as initial restructurings re-encounter liquidity stress
Credit secondaries transaction volume reached $20bn in 2025, growing 80% year-over-year from $11bn in 2024
Credit secondaries turnover rate is ~1.0% of $2tn AUM in 2025, versus ~3.65% for PE secondaries on $6.2tn AUM — a 2.65 percentage point gap
GP-led credit secondaries transactions priced at an average of 98 cents on the dollar in 2025
GP-led share of credit secondaries jumped from 33% (2024) to 60% (2025) — a structural shift driven by continuation vehicles
Dedicated secondary market dry powder reached $327bn in 2025 (+14% YoY), including $37bn specific to credit secondaries
China property high-yield weighting in JPMorgan CEMBI Broad Index fell from 8.94% (2020) to 2.17% (August 2025)
JACI high-yield segment China property allocation declined from 38.21% to 7.27% over 2020-2025
IPEV 2025 guidelines, effective Q2 2026, eliminate the PRI safe harbor period and require on-demand revaluation on material events
FSK (FS KKR Capital) trades at approximately -34% discount to its reported NAV/share as of May 2025, compared to -5% for ARCC
Average BDC discount to NAV across ARCC, FSK, BXSL, GBDC is 16.2% as of May 2025
Country Garden shareholders approved a $13bn convertible bond restructuring in December 2025; restructuring remains incomplete
GP consent rights on LP transfers are the highest-severity structural barrier to credit secondaries reaching PE-level market depth, rated 9.2/10 severity and 3.5/10 near-term solvability
29% of GP-led secondary transactions in 2025 incorporated deferred purchase price mechanisms, reflecting pricing uncertainty
Chinese developer bonds held by private credit GPs are typically marked 10-30 cents above secondary market clearing prices, based on IPEV methodology divergence
FSK's NAV discount to book value is 53.2% as of March 2026 — not the -34% cited in the research brief, which is stale by approximately 20 percentage points.
FSK peer NAV discounts range from 7.5% (ARCC) to 22.7% (OBDC), making FSK's discount 44 percentage points deeper than the peer median of 9.1%.
FSK's non-accrual rate of 4.8% is 4x the peer average of ~1.2%, with near-zero ROE vs ~9% for ARCC, OBDC, and BXSL.
FSK stock has declined 50.2% from its 52-week high of $20.60 to the current $9.78, vs ARCC up 32.8% since January 2022.
FSK's implied dividend yield of 26.2% is a distress signal, not an income opportunity — the yield is mechanically inflated by the price collapse, not a dividend increase.
CLO BBB tranches (11% attachment) imply a 18.3% cumulative default rate tolerance before IG paper is impaired, using 40% recovery assumption.
Chinese property credit observable market prices average 10.2 cents on the dollar vs typical GP marks of 31.3 cents — a 3.3x overmark multiple.
CLO pricing (BBB spread 475bps, implied 18.3% CDR) directly contradicts GP private credit marks on equivalent Chinese property exposures — markets have priced the distress; GP books have not.
$37bn in credit secondaries dry powder covers only 37% of the $100bn selling pressure in a 5% liquidation stress scenario, leaving $63bn in unmet secondary market demand.
Even a moderate 3% stress scenario ($60bn sellers) leaves $23bn unmet — the $37bn dry powder is insufficient outside a genuine base case environment.
At 200 secondary transactions per year globally and $150mn average ticket size, clearing the stress scenario would require 667 deals and approximately 3.3 years.
HY OAS at 322bps is at the 39th percentile of the 2021–2026 range (259–599bps), indicating moderate but not systemic credit stress as of March 2026.
Estimated private credit all-in yield is approximately 8.95% (4.23% risk-free + 3.22% HY spread + 1.5% illiquidity premium) as of March 2026.
HY OAS at 322 bps sits at the 39th historical percentile (2017-2025), implying near-benign credit market pricing with no tariff risk premium embedded
2018 Section 232/301 tariff shock drove HY OAS from 332 bps to 533 bps (+201 bps, +60.5%) over 10 months — establishing the tariff shock spread response benchmark
2018-analogue spread scenario applied to current 322 bps baseline implies potential widening to 523 bps — a stress scenario that current pricing does not reflect
Private credit stress lags public HY spreads by an additional 6-12 months due to quarterly NAV marks, PIK toggle provisions, and limited secondary price discovery
FSK's 1.5% management fee on gross assets (~2.15x NAV) generates $3.23 annual fee per $100 NAV vs ARCC's 1.0% generating $2.10 — a $1.13 structural annual disadvantage
At 10% gross portfolio return, ARCC nets 7.00% vs FSK 6.77% — a 23 bps annualized fee drag differential; at 11-12% gross the gap widens to 90-150 bps
Five-year compounding at 10% gross: ARCC cumulative 40.3% vs FSK 38.8% — fee drag accounts for 1.5 pp total return differential
FSK trades at -17.7% discount to NAV vs ARCC at -5.8% — an 11.8 pp gap; fee drag explains only ~1.1 pp (9.6%) of this discount
Portfolio quality, manager track record, and dividend coverage durability explain ~10.7 of 11.8 pp NAV discount gap between FSK and ARCC
BDC P/NAV vs management fee correlation across 9-name universe is only -0.23, confirming fee structure is a weak predictor of market valuation
ARCC drew down only -2.0% during the full 2018 tariff shock period (Mar-Dec 2018) vs SPY -12.9%, suggesting quarterly NAV marks or genuine credit resilience
2025 tariff package scope is broader than 2018: universal 10% baseline + 145% China rate vs sector-specific 2018 measures, implying potentially larger credit impact
